title: Hasina says she will return to Bangladesh in December even if she is arrested
dek: The former prime minister, in exile in India and sentenced to death in absentia, said she would rather die in her own country. Dhaka says India must extradite her and has ruled out a passport.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Former Bangladeshi prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she will return home from India in December even though she may be arrested, as Dhaka said it would not issue her a passport and that New Delhi must instead extradite her.

"If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people," Hasina said in written answers to questions from an international news agency, published on Thursday. "I know that I may be arrested when I return. I may be imprisoned, tortured or even killed." She did not say how she would travel. Hasina, who fled to India in August 2024, was sentenced to death in her absence last November.

## What Hasina said

"I will return to Bangladesh. That decision has not changed," Hasina said. She has said since the summer that she intends to go back in December. Asked whether the United States or India would press Dhaka to guarantee her safety, she said she was not seeking outside protection: "I do not need the blessing of a foreign power to return to my own country."

She said "there is no normal political or democratic environment" in Bangladesh, and alleged that at least 20,000 members of her Awami League had been killed since August 2024 and thousands arrested, tortured or forced into hiding. That figure has not been independently verified, and the government says those arrested face specific charges. She also said she was concerned about the growing influence of hard-liners. The Prime Minister's Office in Dhaka did not respond to a request for comment, the interviewer reported.

## Dhaka's position

On Thursday, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, said a passport was "not required to bring back terrorists or criminals. It is a matter of handing them over", according to reports. "We are demanding her handover. She should be handed over."

Kobir was speaking after seeing off Liu Haixing, head of the Chinese Communist Party's International Department, at the end of a three-day visit to Dhaka. Asked by reporters whether Hasina had applied for travel documents, he said he did not know, as he had just returned from the Commonwealth summit, one report said. He then dismissed the idea, asking whether she was "coming to visit her in-laws in Rangpur" that Bangladesh should give her a passport.

He called Hasina "a terrorist" and "a fugitive", reports said, and said a judicial warrant, an established legal process and the extradition treaty were enough to secure her return. Bangladesh would keep pursuing it through legal and diplomatic channels, he said.

## Background

Hasina was prime minister for 15 years until a student-led uprising in July and August 2024. A United Nations human rights report estimated that about 1,400 people may have been killed during the crackdown on the protests. In November 2025, Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia, finding that she ordered the crackdown. She denies ordering killings, and her lawyers dispute the toll. Her party, the Awami League, is banned from political activity.

In July this year she said in an interview that she and senior party colleagues planned to return around December and present themselves in court. Tarique Rahman's Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide in the February 2026 election, from which the Awami League was barred.

Dhaka has asked India several times to extradite her. India's Ministry of External Affairs has said the request is being examined under established procedures. On 3 October, India's High Commissioner in Dhaka, Dinesh Trivedi, said the legal process was ongoing and no timeframe could be given because courts were involved, reports said.

## China in the background

At the same send-off, Kobir and Liu discussed a proposed Bangladesh-Myanmar-China economic corridor. Kobir said it could open a new trade and connectivity route, but that stability in Myanmar and a lasting solution to the Rohingya crisis were preconditions for Bangladesh, and he asked for China's continued help with repatriating Rohingya refugees, one report said. The two sides reaffirmed a "China-Bangladesh Community with a Shared Future in the New Era" and noted the results of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to China in June.

During his visit, Liu said work on the Chinese-backed Teesta river project and an industrial zone at Mongla port, both close to India, was "advancing steadily", and invited a delegation of Rahman's Bangladesh Nationalist Party to Beijing.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

Hasina's presence in India has been the biggest irritant in relations with Dhaka since 2024. In August, one report said, citing diplomatic sources, that a visit by Rahman to India hinged on the issue. Relations matter directly to West Bengal, which shares a 2,217 km border with Bangladesh. Pending business includes renewal of the Ganges water-sharing treaty, which expires on 12 December, the long-stalled Teesta agreement, trade through land ports such as Petrapole, and border management.

A firm public line from Dhaka that leaves no route home except extradition makes a quiet compromise harder, while Beijing's party-level courtship of the BNP government continues in parallel.

## What happens next

Bangladesh's parliament begins a session on 9 November. Hasina has named December but given no date or route for her return, and India has given no timeline for a decision on the extradition request.
